data.title: Chotěbuz-Podobora – a Slavic hillfort guarding the ford over the Olša
data.excerpt: The hillfort of Chotěbuz – Podobora stands on a promontory in the Těšín Upland, rising up to 20 m above the ford over the river Olša that it guarded on the trade route through the Moravian Gate. Its three parts – an acropolis and two baileys – were defended by ramparts and ditches, and today the site holds an archaeological open-air museum with a reconstructed box rampart, a gate tower and a bridge over the ditch.
data.metaTitle: Chotěbuz-Podobora – a Slavic hillfort above the Olša ford
data.metaDescription: A Slavic hillfort on a promontory in the Těšín Upland, rising 20 m above the ford over the river Olša; occupied earlier by the Lusatian and Hallstatt cultures.

keyFacts.label: Position
keyFacts.value: About 2 km north-east of the village of Chotěbuz, on a promontory in the Těšín Upland, at an elevation of about 275 m a.s.l.

keyFacts.label: Dimensions of the hillfort
keyFacts.value: Total length about 400 m, width about 110 m, inner area 1.8 ha

keyFacts.label: Layout
keyFacts.value: Three parts — the acropolis and the first and second baileys; the acropolis and the first bailey were the most strongly fortified

keyFacts.label: Defences of the acropolis
keyFacts.value: A timber box rampart on an older Hallstatt rampart, its front wall daubed with clay against fire

keyFacts.label: Ditch of the first bailey
keyFacts.value: 15–17 m wide, pointed in shape, joining a natural gully

keyFacts.label: Cult feature
keyFacts.value: A rectangular timber structure of 3.2 × 5.2 × 5.8 m in the first bailey, with a burnt chest in the middle — probably a pagan sanctuary

keyFacts.label: Another name
keyFacts.value: The hillfort is also called Old Těšín, since the defence of the merchant road through the Moravian Gate was taken over by the later castle at Těšín

keyFacts.label: Today
keyFacts.value: An archaeological open-air museum with a reconstructed box rampart and palisade, an entrance gateway in a tower, a bridge over the ditch and internal buildings

timeline.title: Demise of the Hallstatt hillfort
timeline.description: The hillfort, occupied by the people of the Lusatian culture and later of the Hallstatt culture, was destroyed after repeated attacks; it was renewed only with the arrival of the Slavs.

timeline.title: Arrival of the Slavic population
timeline.description: The Slavs rebuilt the defences on the acropolis and also built the defences of both baileys.

timeline.title: The ditch of the first bailey is dug
timeline.description: A ditch 15–17 m wide, passing smoothly into a natural gully in the north-west.

timeline.title: Loss of the territory north of the Moravian Gate
timeline.description: Violent events accompanied the decline of the realm of the Mojmírids — they are attested by massive burnt layers on the acropolis and in the first bailey, and also by iron arrowheads in the inner palisade of the rampart.

timeline.title: An interruption in occupation of almost a century
timeline.description: After the fires, life at the hillfort ceased for almost the whole century, without any written mentions of the region.

timeline.title: Occupation returns
timeline.description: The hillfort never regained its former importance; the culture of this period is poorer and the occupied area smaller.

timeline.title: Final abandonment of the hillfort
timeline.description: The population moved to Zámocký vrch in present-day Polish Těšín, where a new fortification arose and later the centre of a Piast stronghold district.

children.text: The hillfort of Chotěbuz – Podobora lies about 2 km north-east of the centre of the village in the area of the Těšín Upland and at an elevation of about 275 metres above sea level, on a promontory bounded on the west by a gully with a stream, although for the greater part its edge is formed by a steep drop. In this part the river Olša flowed in the past and there was a ford close by, which was guarded by this very hillfort. The hillfort rises here to a height of up to 20 metres above the surrounding terrain, and so it was very well placed strategically.

The hillfort already played a very important role in the time of the Lusatian culture; later it was occupied in the Hallstatt period, but the most significant occupation can be seen here in the Slavic period, when massive defences were built, above all on the acropolis of the hillfort. When Těšín Castle later became the seat of the Duke of Těšín and the town of Těšín grew up in the settlement below it, the hillfort was abandoned for many centuries. The first reports of archaeological finds from the hillfort date from the 19th century. Later the hillfort became the site of systematic archaeological excavation.

The hillfort came into being as one of the fortified settlements situated along the trade route that linked the north of Europe with its south through the Moravian Gate. For a number of centuries it formed an important seat for the defence of this merchant road, and also a place of trade and a fortified seat for its inhabitants. It came to an end only with the rise of the castle at Těšín. That is why it is also often called Old Těšín.

The total length of the hillfort is about 400 m, its width about 110 m and its inner area 1.8 ha. The hillfort consists of three parts: the acropolis and the first and second baileys. The acropolis and the first bailey were the most strongly fortified. The defences of the second bailey were not completed and are also less visible in the terrain. The eastern side of the hillfort has been affected by landslides. It was probably enclosed only by a light palisade, because natural protection was provided here by the river Olša flowing directly below the hillfort and probably also by the stream on the western side, whose bed is continued by the ditch of the first bailey.
The Hallstatt period

As has already been indicated, the hillfort was first occupied by the people of the Lusatian culture in the Final Bronze Age and later in the Early Iron Age (the Hallstatt culture). In the Hallstatt period the acropolis was occupied, and remains of post-built dwellings, storage pits, pottery and various other finds from this period have been recovered here. The baileys evidently did not form part of the hillfort at that time. In the Hallstatt period the hillfort was attacked by enemies several times, and in the 5th century BC the hillfort was destroyed; life returned within its walls only in the time after the arrival of the Slavs.

children.text: The Slavic period

In the second half of the 8th century a Slavic population came into the area of the hillfort, and life then unfolded fully in it once again. The Slavs rebuilt the defences on the acropolis and also built the defences of both baileys.
The defences

The acropolis at that time was clearly dominated by a massive rampart delimiting its southern part, in front of which there was also a prominent pointed ditch. Originally a timber box rampart stood on the crest of the rampart, which made use of the older Hallstatt rampart and was filled with earth. The front wall of the rampart was daubed with clay, which was intended to prevent any fire. Access to the acropolis across the rampart was secured by a gateway linked to the first bailey, probably by a small bridge. The remainder of the acropolis was protected sufficiently by natural conditions (the steep drop, on which no trees grew, and the river along its sides) for there to be no need to fortify it more substantially. Protection here was probably provided by a palisade fence. The acropolis itself, however, could not accommodate a more numerous Slavic population, and so two further baileys were gradually attached to the acropolis, although the defences of the second were not entirely completed. Each part was fortified separately with ditches and ramparts. The ditches were pointed in shape. The ramparts in the first and second baileys were without an internal structure; on the acropolis, as has already been mentioned, a timber superstructure 4–5 m wide stood on the crown of the older rampart, and in the first bailey the bank was strengthened on both the inner and the outer side by a palisade formed of posts 20–40 cm thick of fir and, to a lesser extent, of oak wood. This wall too was daubed with clay, which was to prevent any fire. The ditch of the first bailey is 15–17 m wide and in the north-west passes smoothly into a natural gully. It evidently came into being in the 8th–9th century. The second bailey too was fortified with a rampart and a ditch 150 m long. Unlike the two preceding parts of the hillfort, the defences of the second bailey are relatively indistinct in the terrain and run from the rampart and ditch of the first bailey in a gentle arc to the drop above the watercourse. These defences evidently came into being in the earlier phase of the Slavic occupation.
The internal buildings of the hillfort

Among the settlement activities of the Slavic period we count above all residential, productive, economic and cult structures. The Slavs covered the area of the acropolis and partly also of the first bailey with a layer of gravel, which was to level out the irregularities in the terrain caused by the preceding occupation and at the same time functioned as a drainage layer (it ensured the drainage of water, so that in times of longer rains there would not be a layer of mud and clay at the hillfort). This gravel layer has, however, meant that today it is not possible to record archaeologically the remains of the structures that stood on the surface of this layer. In the case of sunken features we record only their very lowest part, sunk into the older Hallstatt layer.
Settlement features

Here belong structures built and used by people for dwelling in. These are above all sunken settlement features in which remains of a heating installation (a hearth or an oven) were found. The gaps between the timber logs in all the structures were daubed with clay, which ensured the thermal insulation of the feature. Inside there was a heating installation, and a quantity of charred grain was also found here. A feature was also discovered that was formed by two shallow trodden ovals and the remains of a hearth. We may consider a log-built above-ground structure in the case of this feature.
Productive and economic features

Here we count the remains of structures or installations that served for the production of objects, for the processing and storage of raw materials or foodstuffs, or for the stabling of cattle. These are mostly various small furnaces, a hearth or other heating features, which mostly served for the processing of raw materials, for example the smithing of ore or the production of fired pottery. A further kind are the remains of economic features connected with agricultural production. These are most often storage pits, and features connected with the keeping of domestic animals.
The cult feature

A pagan cult feature was identified at the hillfort, in the first bailey. Archaeological excavation recorded here a rectangular structure open towards the west. The walls of this structure, measuring 3.2 × 5.2 × 5.8 m, were formed of wooden posts, some of which were perhaps not even posts in the true sense of the word, but merely roundwood, evidently intended for sitting on. Roughly in the middle of this grouping a burnt wooden chest measuring 1 × 1 m was uncovered. Whether this chest served for keeping venerated objects, or as the base for the statue of a deity unknown to us, unfortunately cannot be determined with certainty.

The area of present-day Těšín Silesia came into the sphere of influence of Great Moravia and for a certain time was also part of it. Some time at the turn of the 9th and 10th centuries, or at the very beginning of the 10th century, in connection with the declining realm of the Mojmírids, when the peripheral territories in particular sought to break away, the loss of the territories north of the Moravian Gate also occurred. That this did not take place without bloodshed and violence is betrayed by the massive burnt layers on the acropolis and in the first bailey, but also, for example, by the iron arrowheads in the inner palisade of the rampart. After these turbulent events, life at the hillfort ceased for almost the whole of the 10th century, for which we have no written mentions of this region either. Only in the last quarter of that century did occupation return to the site. The hillfort, however, never regained its former lustre. The culture of this period too is relatively poorer and the occupied area smaller. The inhabitants lived in rectangular sunken-featured buildings covered with a gabled roof. They made their living by growing grain and keeping cattle.

children.text: At roughly the middle of the 11th century the hillfort was gradually abandoned by its inhabitants. In the given political situation a position pushed forward immediately above the right bank of the river Olša, on Zámocký vrch in present-day Polish Těšín, proved more viable; there, in the course of the second half of the 10th century, an entirely new fortification arose on older prehistoric foundations, which relatively soon became an important centre of one of the Piast stronghold districts in Silesia.
The hillfort today – the archaeological open-air museum
Today at the hillfort you will find an
archaeological open-air museum

which in my opinion has the best-reconstructed rampart of all the Slavic open-air museums. Besides the box rampart and the palisade, the entrance gateway in the defensive tower is also delightful, as are the bridge over the ditch and the expanding internal buildings, which consist of several dwelling houses, pottery kilns and a pagan sanctuary. At weekends and on public holidays your visit will be made especially engaging and interesting by the historical group
Tizon

which brings life in the Slavic period closer to visitors. You will witness not only fighting, but you will also see a smith and traders at work, and you will learn a great deal about the pagan deities of the Slavs. I warmly recommend a visit to the hillfort.
